title: Ken Paxton’s Anti-Abortion Influence Already Extended Beyond Texas. He Could Take It Further in the Senate.
author: Cassandra Jaramillo
content:
Early in his tenure as Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton issued [a
statement](https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/news/releases/attorney-
general-paxton-statement-roe-v-wade-anniversary) commemorating what he
believed was a national tragedy.

“It’s impossible to fill the void of more than 50 million missing human
beings,” he said in 2016. He was marking the 43rd anniversary of Roe v. Wade,
the Supreme Court ruling that protected abortion rights — and had long stood
in the way of efforts to ban terminations in early pregnancy, when most
abortions occur.

Paxton spent the years that followed testing Roe’s limits and ultimately
prevailed where others had failed: In 2021, he defended a near-total abortion
ban that Texas legislators had designed to evade conventional legal
challenges. The U.S. Supreme Court allowed it to take effect while Roe
remained in force.

After the justices overturned Roe the following year, Paxton kept pushing,
pursuing new ways to extend the reach of Texas' restrictions. He prevailed
against the Biden administration, picked fights with states that protect
abortion access and pioneered strategies that his peers later adopted or
expanded.

While Paxton’s tenure as attorney general has drawn criticism from across the
political spectrum for his [personal
scandals](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/07/10/angela-paxton-divorce-texas-
attorney-general-ken/) and alleged [misuse of the
office](https://www.texastribune.org/2020/11/13/whistleblower-lawsuit-texas-
ken-paxton/), detractors and allies alike agree that his signal achievement as
the state's top legal official has been advancing restrictions on abortion.

A close look at his record shows a clear pattern in his successes: He
relentlessly tests the limits of the law and employs novel legal strategies to
advance his goals.

Paxton’s national role as an anti-abortion warrior would change if he wins his
U.S. Senate race. As Texas attorney general, he has been able to act largely
on his own authority. If he prevails in November, he would become one of 100
senators in a chamber where most legislation needs 60 votes to overcome a
filibuster.

But allies who have witnessed his victories see an opening.

“He’ll have the ability to use some of the laws that he’s defended in Texas as
influence to draft legislation in the U.S. Senate,” said Mary Elizabeth
Castle, director of government relations at Texas Values, a Christian advocacy
group that supports a national abortion ban.

Legal experts and advocates on both sides expect he could join colleagues who
are pressuring the Food and Drug Administration to revoke its approval of the
abortion drug mifepristone.

Anti-abortion activists at the state and federal level are also trying to
secure legal rights for fetuses, which could have implications for
reproductive care like birth control and in vitro fertilization. Paxton, who
has called himself a strong supporter of IVF, recently said he was open to
restrictions intended to prevent the loss of fertilized eggs.

His litigation has also raised questions that experts expect the Supreme Court
to confront, including whether a federal law, which mandates hospitals provide
stabilizing care to patients having an emergency, overrides state abortion
bans; whether to treat a fetus as a separate patient that has its own
emergency care rights; and how far states can go in pursuing out-of-state
doctors who prescribe abortion medication to patients in states where it’s
banned.

During the current race, abortion has played a far smaller role than questions
about Paxton’s ethics. His Democratic opponent, James Talarico, has said that
he supports restoring a federal right to abortion and that his Christian faith
calls for an end to “extreme” laws that Paxton has defended and that have
forced women to flee the state for emergency abortion care.

Lately, Paxton has said little about abortion — an issue on which he has
defended [restrictions more stringent](https://www.tpr.org/government-
politics/2025-02-07/a-majority-of-texans-say-abortions-should-be-allowed-in-
cases-of-rape-and-incest-in-new-poll) than [many Texans say they
want](https://texaspolitics.utexas.edu/set/should-abortion-laws-in-texas-be-
more-or-less-strict-june-2026).

But those who have watched Paxton extend the reach of Texas law beyond its
borders are paying close attention to his Senate bid.

Dr. Jennifer Villavicencio, an abortion provider, said she has felt compelled
to move her family twice to states with strong laws shielding doctors from
out-of-state litigation, partly out of concern that Paxton is creating a
blueprint for targeting providers like her.

“It’s very disheartening and scary to think that it’s maybe coming to the U.S.
Senate,” she said.

Lisa Larson-Walker/ProPublica. Source images: Drew Angerer/Getty Images, Tasos

### Paxton successfully defended a near-total abortion ban before Roe v. Wade
was struck down.

When Paxton became Texas attorney general in 2015, there was no ambiguity
about where he stood on abortion.

Raised by [an anti-abortion
activist](https://www.beckerfuneral.com/obituary/sally-paxton), he married his
sweetheart from a Christian college, who spoke proudly about the fact that she
was [adopted](https://x.com/AngelaPaxtonTX/status/1934235907583889615?s=20),
saying her birth mother “[chose
life](https://www.texastribune.org/2023/05/28/texas-angela-paxton/).” She
campaigned for Paxton, but he had his own bona fides. A law he’d co-sponsored
as a state senator banned almost all abortions after 20 weeks.

Similar 20-week bans had taken root across the country as decades of court
rulings chipped away at Roe, but no state had managed to enforce a ban as
early as six weeks. More than a dozen tried, passing laws that prohibited
abortion when cardiac activity could be detected. One after another, they were
blocked by judges.

Then, in 2021, a Texas lawyer named Jonathan Mitchell worked with legislators
to craft a law that would withstand similar challenges. Instead of having
state officials enforce their “heartbeat law,” the new act, referred to as
Senate Bill 8, allowed citizens to sue physicians they suspected were
providing abortions. The law offered up to $10,000 if they won.

When abortion providers and President Joe Biden’s administration separately
challenged the law in federal court, Paxton’s office argued that state
officials couldn’t be ordered to stop enforcing it because they had no power
to do so in the first place. Only private citizens could.

“Because the executive officials are expressly prohibited from enforcing SB
8,” his office wrote to the Supreme Court, “there is nothing for a federal
court to enjoin.”

The Supreme Court agreed that Paxton couldn’t be sued because “the petitioners
have not identified any enforcement authority the attorney general possesses
in connection with S. B. 8 that a federal court might enjoin him from
exercising.”

The law remained in effect, becoming the first enforceable six-week ban under
Roe.

Legislators in [Idaho](https://apnews.com/article/idaho-abortion-ban-
law-6eec10650b51c2b9dc98607d13cd8f40) and
[Oklahoma](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/oklahoma-abortion-ban-bill-governor/)
subsequently passed similar laws.

For Dr. Sam Dickman, who worked at a San Antonio Planned Parenthood, the
implications were clear: “I was going to need to either entirely change the
type of medicine I was providing or leave the state,” he said. He opted for
the latter, moving to Montana, where abortion is legal until viability, or
roughly 24 weeks.

Days after the Texas ban took effect, [Josseli Barnica arrived at a Houston
hospital in the midst of a
miscarriage](https://www.propublica.org/article/josseli-barnica-death-
miscarriage-texas-abortion-ban). She was 17 weeks pregnant and her fetus’s
head was pressed up against her dilated cervix. Because the situation put her
at high risk of developing an infection, medical experts said doctors should
have offered to speed up delivery or empty her uterus; the fetus was not
viable, and losing the pregnancy was inevitable.

But the fetus’s heart was still beating.

Barnica relayed to her husband what she said her medical providers had told
her: “They had to wait until there was no heartbeat,” he told ProPublica in
Spanish. “It would be a crime to give her an abortion.”

For 40 hours, Barnica waited, her uterus exposed to bacteria.

She died days later of sepsis. Medical experts told ProPublica her doctors did
not follow the proper standard of care and that Barnica’s death was
preventable.

In a statement, HCA Healthcare, the hospital chain that treated her, said “our
responsibility is to be in compliance with applicable state and federal laws
and regulations” and said that physicians exercise their independent judgment.

### Paxton blocked federal guidance for emergency abortion care, with
consequences far beyond Texas.

When the Supreme Court overturned the constitutional right to abortion on June
24, 2022, Paxton dismissed his staff at noon to celebrate. He would later
designate the date as a paid office holiday, Sanctity of Life Day.

The Texas Legislature had prepared for the occasion, passing a law that went
into effect shortly after the overturning of Roe. The ban threatened doctors
with up to 99 years in prison if they performed an abortion. But soon came
what Paxton framed as a federal attempt to thwart the state law.

The Biden administration issued a memo to doctors in states with abortion bans
saying that a federal emergency care law protected their medical judgment,
“regardless of the restrictions in the state.”

The federal Health and Human Services secretary at the time said doctors had
an obligation to follow the Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act,
better known as EMTALA. The law requires hospitals that accept federal funding
to screen and stabilize every patient who arrives.

For those with complications such as severe preeclampsia, a potentially fatal,
pregnancy-related blood pressure disorder, stabilizing a patient might require
performing an abortion, even if the state forbids it, the guidance said. “The
physician must provide that treatment,” it said, bolding the word “must.”

Paxton sued, accusing the administration of an attempt to use federal law “to
transform every emergency room in the country into a walk-in abortion clinic.”

He argued EMTALA was created to make sure hospitals didn’t dump uninsured
patients back on the street without treatment, not to override state laws. He
took the argument a step further, suggesting that under EMTALA, doctors might
need to consider “the life of the unborn child.”

The argument was novel, six legal experts told ProPublica.

“He’s basically suing the federal government to protect Texas’ right to force
pregnant women to not get abortions, even when their health is threatened,”
said Greer Donley, a law professor at the University of Pittsburgh. “I
remember thinking, ‘Wow, that’s radical.’”

Medical groups warned patients would die.

But a federal judge sided with Paxton that August, and the 5th U.S. Circuit
Court of Appeals affirmed the decision in January 2024.

The ruling did more than keep the administration from enforcing its EMTALA
interpretation in Texas.

It barred the federal government from pursuing cases against members of two
anti-abortion medical organizations that had joined Paxton’s suit as
plaintiffs, the American Association of Pro-Life Obstetricians and
Gynecologists and the Christian Medical & Dental Associations. This
effectively exempted them from having to follow the federal guidance,
regardless of where they worked.

It also served as immediate litigation fodder for another state fighting to
enforce its own abortion ban.

Idaho had not had the same success in court as Texas. After the Biden
administration sued, arguing the state’s ban conflicted with EMTALA, Idaho
lost in lower and appellate courts, leaving its ban effectively frozen in
emergency cases, with doctors instructed to follow the federal guidance.

But Paxton’s 5th Circuit win on Jan. 2, 2024, gave Idaho’s ban a lifeline. The
ruling conflicted with the 9th Circuit's decision in Idaho, creating the kind
of disagreement between federal appeals courts that the Supreme Court often
steps in to resolve.

The following day, attorneys representing Idaho asked the high court to do
just that, saying Paxton’s success showed they were “likely to prevail.” In
the meantime, they asked the court to unfreeze the ban.

On Jan. 5, the Supreme Court allowed Idaho to fully enforce its ban while the
case proceeded.

Emergency doctors began hesitating over when they could legally provide
abortions, Dr. Jim Souza, chief physician at St. Luke's Health System, [said
on a press call at the time, according to
NPR](https://www.npr.org/2024/04/25/1246990306/more-emergency-flights-for-
pregnant-patients--in-idaho). “Is she septic enough for me to do this abortion
and not risk going to jail and losing my license?”

In the three months that followed, St. Luke’s, the state’s largest hospital
system, said it had to airlift six patients out of the state for abortions.

In Texas, ProPublica has documented the consequences for women experiencing
pregnancy emergencies.

When Tierra Walker sought care later that year in San Antonio, she [developed
preeclampsia and ultimately died from
it](https://www.propublica.org/article/texas-abortion-ban-tierra-walker-
preeclampsia), ProPublica previously reported. None of the 90 physicians
involved in her care offered her the option of terminating her pregnancy, even
after she asked if doing so might keep her safe.

Her family sued Paxton in September, along with state medical officials and
several healthcare providers, alleging that Texas’ abortion restrictions and
the care Walker received led to her death. Paxton has not responded to the
suit and did not respond to a request seeking comment.

ProPublica has identified [at least two
other](https://www.propublica.org/article/nevaeh-crain-death-texas-abortion-
ban-emtala) pregnant [Texas women](https://www.propublica.org/article/porsha-
ngumezi-miscarriage-death-texas-abortion-ban) who died without what experts
said was appropriate emergency care. Paxton has not publicly commented on any
of their deaths and did not respond to ProPublica’s questions about them. Our
analysis also found [worsening
outcomes](https://www.propublica.org/article/texas-abortion-ban-sepsis-
maternal-mortality-analysis) across [the
state](https://www.propublica.org/article/texas-abortion-ban-miscarriage-
blood-transfusions) for patients experiencing [pregnancy
complications](https://www.propublica.org/article/ectopic-pregnancy-deaths-
doubled-analysis).

The reach of Paxton’s legal victory may not end there.

The Supreme Court still hasn’t resolved the conflict between the circuit
rulings. It declined to do so in the Idaho case, and after President Donald
Trump took office, his administration dropped the suit and rescinded the
EMTALA guidance.

But legal experts told ProPublica the Supreme Court has yet to resolve core
questions that Paxton’s litigation raised: whether EMTALA preempts state
abortion laws and whether a fetus also has a right to emergency treatment that
could conflict with the mother’s interests in cases where her health is at
risk.

To guard against future rulings, a reproductive rights advocacy group called
All* Above All is pushing state-level legislation to safeguard emergency care.
“We're seeing the chaos right now and the confusion," said its president,
Nourbese Flint.

### Paxton tested expansive new ways to pursue abortion providers. Other
states are following his lead.

On Dec. 7, 2023, a state judge in Austin issued a ruling that Paxton
immediately moved to stop.

A 31-year-old mother named Kate Cox wanted permission to get an abortion. She
was 20 weeks pregnant and carrying a fetus diagnosed with trisomy 18, a
genetic condition that kills the vast majority of babies born with it.

Texas doesn’t allow abortions for fatal fetal anomalies, but Cox’s doctor
argued that if she was forced to give birth, it could imperil her ability to
get pregnant again. It was also medically risky: Cox had already had two
children by cesarean section, and the chances of complications increase with
each procedure.

The day a Travis County district court judge granted her request, Paxton took
a step legal experts told ProPublica they had not seen another state attorney
general take:

He sent letters to three hospitals where Cox’s doctor had admitting
privileges, threatening legal action if the doctor performed the abortion a
judge said she could have. The court order, he wrote, did not insulate
hospitals, doctors or anyone else from civil and criminal liability for
violating Texas’ abortion laws.

At the same time, he appealed the case to the Texas Supreme Court, saying that
Cox did not face the kind of threat to her life that fell under the law’s
exception. If legislators had wanted to write an exception for fatal fetal
anomalies, he said, they would have done so.

“The Texas Legislature did not intend for courts to become revolving doors of
permission slips to obtain abortions,” he said.

The Texas Supreme Court agreed with Paxton and reversed the lower court’s
ruling. By that time, Cox had sought an abortion out of state.

“It was incredibly scary,” Cox told ProPublica. “We saw in my case that Texas
will go after doctors.”

Paxton was also the first — and, so far, the only — attorney general to
criminally prosecute a provider in his state for violating an abortion ban.

According to court documents, investigators got an anonymous tip alleging that
abortions were being performed at a medical clinic that catered to low-income,
Spanish-speaking patients, managed by Maria Rojas, a licensed midwife.

Rojas was arrested and charged with practicing medicine without a license and
violating the state’s abortion ban. Paxton also moved to temporarily shut down
the clinic and others she ran while the case progressed through court. Months
after her arrest, Paxton announced [he had arrested and indicted
eight](https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/news/releases/attorney-general-
paxton-arrests-eight-individuals-including-foreign-nationals-connected-
houston) other clinic staffers for practicing medicine without a license.

Rojas has pleaded not guilty to the charges. Her attorneys have accused
Paxton’s office of a shoddy investigation and argued that at least one case
prosecutors were treating as an abortion was actually the management of a
patient’s miscarriage.

A trial has not yet been scheduled, but an appeals court this summer
overturned the order shuttering the clinics, finding the state had not
presented sufficient admissible evidence to justify a temporary injunction.
Paxton said he is appealing the ruling. The court did not rule on whether
Rojas had actually performed illegal abortions.

Paxton has not stopped at the state border in his pursuit of doctors.

In December 2024, he sued Dr. Margaret Carpenter, a New York-based physician,
accusing her of violating multiple Texas laws when she treated a patient via
telehealth who lived in Plano, a suburb north of Dallas, and prescribed her
abortion medication.

Because the patient was based in Texas, he argued, Carpenter was subject to
laws there that banned abortion and required a license to practice in the
state.

Carpenter didn’t respond to the suit, so Paxton won by default. But Texas was
unable to collect on more than $100,000 in civil fines and court fees that
resulted; a New York county clerk refused to register the judgment, invoking a
“shield law” that protects providers of abortion care that is legal in New
York from certain out-of-state investigations, prosecutions and judgments. At
least 22 states have passed shield laws since Roe was overturned, and New
York’s is among the strongest. Carpenter did not respond to a request seeking
comment and has not publicly responded to the case.

A New York judge dismissed Paxton’s case seeking to enforce the judgment, but
Paxton didn’t give up, filing two more civil suits this year against
practitioners and organizations in Delaware and California that mail abortion
medication to Texas.

Three other state attorneys general have now expanded on the strategy. Last
month, Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill — who brought criminal charges
against Carpenter after Paxton sued her ([and has faced similar obstacles in
New York](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/ny-gov-hochul-rejects-
louisiana-extradition-doctor-abortion-pill-case-rcna192156)) — joined the
attorneys general of Arkansas and Alabama in filing a sweeping federal civil
suit against out-of-state providers of abortion pills. The case names some of
the same providers Paxton pursued; they have challenged the suits. The three
attorneys general filed a separate action directly with the Supreme Court
asking it to strike down shield laws in New York, Massachusetts and
California.

Paxton has moved beyond doctors to target other entities that help patients
obtain abortions. Mary Ziegler, an abortion historian and professor of law at
University of California, Davis, called him “an innovator in terms of
broadening the network of people who were seen as culprits or aiders or
abettors.”

He sent cease-and-desist letters to organizations that ship abortion
medication into Texas; the attorney general of Alabama subsequently used
similar tactics. And Paxton sued cities in his state to stop them from
disbursing funds to help women travel for abortions — a move the Legislature
followed with a law banning such funding.

Following his legal victory against the city of San Antonio early this year,
in which it was forced to end the $100,000 program, Paxton [made a
vow](https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/news/releases/attorney-general-ken-
paxton-secures-victory-against-san-antonio-after-city-illegally-tried-fund-
out):

“I will always do everything in my power to prevent radicals from manipulating
the system to murder innocent babies.”
